desc:
Teachers write feedback reports about students. Words are encoded as integers: positive lists the ids of positive words and negative the ids of negative words (no id is in both lists; any other word id is neutral).

Each row of reports is [studentId, w1, w2, ...]: one report about student studentId that contains the words w1, w2, ... (a row may contain only the student id). A student can be the subject of many reports. Every occurrence of a positive word adds 3 points, every occurrence of a negative word subtracts 1 point, neutral words add nothing.

Return the ids of the k students with the highest total score, ordered by score from high to low, and by smaller id first when scores are equal. Only students who appear in at least one report take part.

positive = [1, 2], negative = [3]
reports = [[10,1,3], [20,2,2], [10,3,3,4], [30,4]], k = 2
student 10: +3 -1 -1 +0 = 1,  student 20: +6,  student 30: 0
answer = [20, 10]
constraints: 1 ≤ reports.length ≤ 500; every row has between 1 and 40 numbers
1 ≤ k ≤ number of distinct students in reports
hints: First compute one total score per student: a dictionary from student id to score, updated word by word for every report.
Ranking is by (score descending, id ascending). Turn it into a key where 'worse' simply means 'smaller'.
Push (score, -id) into a min-heap of size k and pop whenever it grows past k; at the end sort the survivors from best to worst.
editorial: Put the positive and negative word ids into sets for O(1) lookup. Walk through every report and add +3, -1 or 0 per word to the student's total.

To select the k best students use a min-heap of size k whose entries are (score, -id). A smaller tuple means a worse student: a lower score, or the same score with a larger id. After each push, evict the smallest when the heap has more than k entries. When all students have been seen, sort the heap in descending order and read off the ids.

Scoring costs O(total words); selection costs O(S log k) for S distinct students. A plain sort of all students by (-score, id) is O(S log S) and equally correct; the heap version is the one to know when S is huge and k is small.
